_comment: THE source of the "When will I use this?" section (contract WHEN-WILL-I-USE-THIS, Jon, 10 and 22 Nov 2026).
scripts/build-uses.py writes every page under when-will-i-use-this/ from this file; scripts/check-uses.py (CI) fails a page that differs,
and recomputes every worked step with "=". Never edit a generated page: edit this file, run build-uses.py, then check-uses.py.
topics: slug, title, answer (the one-line answer), keywords (matched exactly against data/games.json's game keywords for "Practise it";
only live games, outside the roster's Unlisted and Withdrawn sections), parentGuide (a folder under parents/, or null).
routes: the 15 Skills England routes, slug, exact name and colour (white text on it at 4.5:1 or better; one per route, distinct,
never the portal's teal: WWIUT-STAND-OUT). A route page is written only for a route with a scenario.
scenarios: id, topic, route (a route slug, or null), job, tier ("F" Foundation GCSE, "H" Higher GCSE or "L4" Level 4:
a Higher or Level 4 card shows a small tag; WWIUT-BATCH-1-2), headline (the key sum, shown after the steps on the job's
own section as "The answer:", recomputed by check-uses.py like a step), formula, formulaNote, question, inside,
text, steps, sources [{title, url, type}], exampleFigures.
formula (WWIUT-CARD-FORMAT): the school-shaped equation the job uses, in LaTeX, or null; set large, first, on its hub
card and its job section. formulaNote (optional): a short line naming its letters, small under it. question: the job's
question, ending "?", shown on the card in place of the worked sum. inside: the topic tag the card shows as "Inside: ...".
The scenarios' text and steps are the approved wording (10 Nov 2026), verbatim: never reword them to fit the format.
A step is a string, or {"text": ..., "noCheck": "<one-line reason>"} when check-uses.py cannot read one of its "=" signs.
exampleFigures is true exactly when the wording marks a figure "(example figure)" or "(example figures)".
Only source type "public" is valid in v1 (a contributor type needs Jon's ruling on consent and naming).

scenarios.headline: 0.3 ÷ 6 = 0.05 m³ per part
scenarios.question: How much cement goes in 0.3 m³ of concrete?
scenarios.text: Concrete for a shed base is often mixed 1 : 2 : 3: 1 part cement, 2 parts sand, 3 parts gravel, in buckets of the same size. You need 0.3 m³ of dry mix.
steps: Cement 0.05 m³, sand 0.10 m³, gravel 0.15 m³.

sources.title: Jewson, "How to make concrete"

scenarios.headline: 40 × 2 = 80 g of developer
scenarios.question: How much developer for 40 g of colour?
scenarios.text: Colour is mixed with developer in the ratio the maker gives. Wella's Koleston Perfect is mixed 1 : 1, but its Special Blonde shades are mixed 1 : 2. You use 40 g of a Special Blonde shade.

steps.noCheck: A ratio, not a sum: there is nothing on the left to recompute.

sources.title: Wella Professionals, Koleston Perfect usage booklet

scenarios.headline: 125 ÷ 250 × 5 = 2.5 ml
scenarios.question: How many ml is a 125 mg dose?
scenarios.text: Liquid medicine comes at a strength, such as 250 mg in 5 ml. Nurses use: volume = what you want ÷ what you have × what it is in. The prescription is 125 mg. The bottle says 250 mg in 5 ml.

sources.title: Gloucestershire Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, Intravenous Drug and Fluid Administration Training: calculation practice formulae

scenarios.question: What goes on the bill once VAT is added?
scenarios.text: A VAT-registered plumber adds 20% VAT to the bill. To add 20%, multiply by 1.2. The job costs £350 before VAT.

sources.title: GOV.UK, "VAT rates" (rate checked 10 Nov 2026)

scenarios.question: Will this lighting circuit pass inspection?
scenarios.text: Voltage drops along a long cable. The wiring rules (BS 7671) allow at most 3% on a lighting circuit and 5% on others. The UK supply is 230 V.

steps.text: Most allowed on lighting: 3% of 230 = 0.03 × 230 = 6.9 V.
steps.noCheck: "3% of 230" uses "of", which the check does not read; 0.03 × 230 = 6.9 is still recomputed.

steps: A lighting circuit drops 5.4 V. As a percentage: 5.4 ÷ 230 × 100 = 2.3%.

sources.title: NICEIC, "Calculating voltage drop" (Professional Electrician), citing BS 7671 Appendix 4
Skills England, Installation and maintenance electrician (OCC0152), route Construction and the built environment

scenarios.headline: 0.7 × 500 = 350 g of water
scenarios.question: How much water for 500 g of flour?
scenarios.text: Bakers write recipes in "baker's percentages": the flour is always 100%, and everything else is a percentage of the flour's weight. A dough is 70% water and 2% salt. You use 500 g of flour.

steps.noCheck: "70% of 500" uses "of", which the check does not read; 0.7 × 500 = 350 is still recomputed.
"2% of 500" uses "of", which the check does not read; 0.02 × 500 = 10 is still recomputed.

sources.title: King Arthur Baking, "Baker's percentage"

scenarios.headline: 4 × 0.375 = 1.5 g of gold
scenarios.question: How much real gold is in a 9 carat ring?
scenarios.text: Gold is measured in carats out of 24. 9 carat gold is 9 parts gold in 24. The UK hallmark writes it as 375: 375 parts gold in every 1000.
steps: A 9 carat ring weighs 4 g. Gold in it: 4 × 0.375 = 1.5 g.

sources.title: Assay Office London, hallmarking guidance

scenarios.headline: 64 ÷ 16 = 4 litres
scenarios.formulaNote: P is the perimeter, h the height
scenarios.question: How many litres to paint this room?
scenarios.text: A room is 4 m by 3.5 m, with walls 2.5 m high. There is a 2 m² door and a 3.5 m² window. Two coats; the tin says 1 litre covers 16 m² (example figure).
steps: Take away door and window: 37.5 − 5.5 = 32 m².

sources.title: Dulux, "How much paint do you need?"

scenarios.headline: 2 × (100 + 64) = 328 m of line
scenarios.question: How much white line does a full-size pitch need?
scenarios.text: Groundspeople mark out pitches. The FA's recommended adult pitch is 100 m long and 64 m wide.
steps: Lines round the edge (perimeter): 2 × (100 + 64) = 328 m of white line.

sources.title: The FA, "Guide to pitch and goalpost dimensions"
Skills England, Sports turf operative standard (ST0210), which lists marking out playing surfaces

scenarios.headline: 3 × 150 = 450 kg
scenarios.question: How much fertiliser does this field need?
scenarios.text: Fertiliser is spread at a rate in kg per hectare. 1 hectare = 10 000 m². A field is 250 m by 120 m; the plan is 150 kg per hectare (example figure).

steps.noCheck: 30 000 m² = 3 ha is a change of unit (1 hectare = 10 000 m²), not a sum; 250 × 120 = 30 000 is still recomputed.

sources.title: AHDB, Nutrient Management Guide (RB209), which gives every rate in kg/ha

scenarios.question: Why isn't one blood pressure reading enough?
scenarios.text: One blood pressure reading can mislead, so NICE says to take readings at home, twice a day for 4 to 7 days, ignore the first day, and use the mean of the rest. After day 1, the top (systolic) numbers are 138, 134, 136, 140, 132, 136 (example figures).
steps: The doctor compares that average, with the clinic reading, against NICE's limits.

sources.title: NICE guideline NG136, Hypertension in adults

scenarios.headline: 100 − 91 = 9 in 100 weigh more
scenarios.question: What does "the 91st centile" mean for this baby?
scenarios.text: Babies' weights are plotted on growth charts with centile lines. A centile shows how many healthy children are expected to be below that line. A baby is on the 91st centile.
steps: 91 out of 100 healthy babies the same age are expected to weigh less.
100 − 91 = 9 out of 100 are expected to weigh more.

sources.title: Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, UK-WHO growth charts

scenarios.headline: 4 × 1500 = 6000 orchids
scenarios.question: How many orchids are in this meadow, without counting them?
scenarios.text: You can't count every wild orchid in a meadow, so ecologists count them in a few 1 m² squares (quadrats) placed at random, and scale up. Ten quadrats count 3, 5, 2, 4, 6, 3, 4, 5, 2, 6 (example figures). The meadow is 1500 m².

sources.title: Oak National Academy, "Estimating population size using quadrats"
Skills England occupational map (Ecologist)

scenarios.headline: 9.1 − 8.3 = 0.8 °C warmer
scenarios.question: How much warmer is a "normal" UK year now?
scenarios.text: "Warmer than average" means compared with a 30-year average. The Met Office now uses 1991–2020.
steps: How a mean works: five Julys of 19.2, 20.1, 18.7, 21.3 and 19.7 °C (example figures) total 99.0; mean 99.0 ÷ 5 = 19.8 °C.

sources.title: Met Office, climate averages notes
Met Office, "How have daily temperatures shifted in the UK's changing climate?"

scenarios.headline: (42 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100 = 5% better
scenarios.question: Has six weeks' training actually worked?
scenarios.text: Sports scientists analyse training data to see if an athlete is improving. One jump can be a fluke, so they use the mean of several. Five jumps before training: 38, 41, 39, 42, 40 cm (example figures). After six weeks the mean is 42 cm.

sources.title: National Careers Service, "Performance sports scientist"

scenarios.headline: 0.2 × 1452.50 = £290.50 tax
scenarios.question: How much tax comes off a £2,500 month?
scenarios.text: Payroll works out the tax taken from each month's pay. In 2026 to 2027 the first £12,570 a year is tax-free and the next band is taxed at 20%. Someone earns £2,500 this month (example figure). National Insurance is worked out separately. Real payslips use HMRC's tax tables, so they can differ by a few pence.

steps.noCheck: "20% of 1452.50" uses "of", which the check does not read; 0.2 × 1452.50 = 290.50 is still recomputed.

sources.title: GOV.UK, "Income Tax rates and Personal Allowances" (tax year 6 April 2026 to 5 April 2027)

scenarios.headline: 9000 − 3000 = £6,000 to HMRC
scenarios.formulaNote: S is sales, P is purchases, before VAT
scenarios.question: How much does this business owe HMRC?
scenarios.text: Every three months a business tells HMRC the VAT it charged customers and the VAT it paid suppliers, and pays the difference. Sales of £45,000 and purchases of £15,000 this quarter, before VAT, all at 20% (example figures).

sources.title: GOV.UK, "How to fill in and submit your VAT Return (VAT Notice 700/12)"

scenarios.headline: 0.2 × 19430 = £3,886 to set aside
scenarios.question: How much should you put aside for tax?
scenarios.text: No boss takes tax off for you, so you set money aside yourself. Same 2026 to 2027 rules: £12,570 tax-free, then 20%. This year's profit is £32,000 (example figure). National Insurance comes on top.

sources.title: GOV.UK, "Income Tax rates and Personal Allowances"

scenarios.question: What do we pay back for 140 miles?
scenarios.text: Staff who use their own car for work are paid mileage. For 2026 to 2027 the approved rate is 55p a mile for the first 10,000 miles (it was 45p). A member of staff drove 140 business miles this month (example figure).

sources.title: GOV.UK, "Increasing mileage rates" (2026 to 2027)

scenarios.headline: 25.00 + 0.05 = 25.05 mm, the most it can be
scenarios.question: Does a 25.07 mm shaft pass?
scenarios.text: Drawings give a size and a tolerance: how far off it may be and still pass. A shaft must be 25.00 mm ± 0.05 mm. You measure 25.07 mm.
steps: 25.07 is bigger than 25.05, so it fails.

sources.title: National Careers Service, "CNC machinist"
Skills England, Machining technician (OCC1305)

scenarios.headline: 2000 ÷ 230 = 8.7 A
scenarios.question: 3 A or 13 A fuse for a toaster?
scenarios.text: A plug fuse must be big enough for the appliance's current. Current = power ÷ voltage, I = P ÷ V. UK mains is 230 V.
steps: Toaster, 2000 W: I = 2000 ÷ 230 = 8.7 A, too much for a 3 A fuse, so 13 A.
Lamp, 60 W: I = 60 ÷ 230 = 0.26 A, so a 3 A fuse is fine.

sources.title: Electrical Safety First, "Plugs and fuses"

scenarios.headline: 48 ÷ 16 = 3 wheel turns per pedal turn
scenarios.question: Which gear gets you up the hill?
scenarios.text: The gear ratio is the chainring's teeth ÷ the rear cog's teeth: how many times the back wheel turns for one turn of the pedals.
steps: Change to a 32-tooth cog for hills: 48 ÷ 32 = 1.5 turns, easier to pedal, slower.

sources.title: Sheldon Brown, "Gain ratios"
National Careers Service, "Cycle mechanic"
Skills England, Bicycle mechanic (OCC0622)

scenarios.formulaNote: n is the number of sides
scenarios.question: Why do hexagon tiles fit, but pentagons don't?
scenarios.text: Tiles fit with no gaps only if the angles meeting at each corner add up to 360°.
steps: A regular hexagon's angle: (6 − 2) × 180 ÷ 6 = 120°. Three meet: 3 × 120 = 360°, so they fit.
A regular pentagon's angle is 108°: 360 ÷ 108 = 3.33, not a whole number, so gaps.

sources.title: Skills England, Wall and floor tiler (OCC0368)
National Careers Service, "Tiler"

scenarios.headline: 600 × 8 ÷ 80 = 60 seconds
scenarios.question: How long will a 600 MB update take?
scenarios.text: Broadband is sold in megabits per second (Mbit/s), but files are measured in megabytes (MB). 8 megabits = 1 megabyte. A 600 MB update on an 80 Mbit/s line (example figures):

sources.title: Local Government Association, glossary (8 megabits = 1 megabyte)
National Careers Service, "IT support technician"

scenarios.headline: 270 ÷ 50 = 5.4 hours
scenarios.question: Does this run need a legal break?
scenarios.text: Lorry drivers must take a 45-minute break after 4½ hours of driving. A 270-mile run at an average of 50 mph (example figures):

steps.noCheck: Hours and minutes ("5 h 24 min") are not read by the check; 270 ÷ 50 = 5.4 is still recomputed.

steps.text: That's over 4½ hours, so a 45-minute break goes in: 5 h 24 min + 45 min = 6 h 09 min door to door.
steps.noCheck: Hours and minutes (5 h 24 min + 45 min = 6 h 09 min) are not read by the check.

sources.title: GOV.UK / DVSA, "Drivers' hours: HGV driver basics"

scenarios.headline: 1350 − 1500 = −150 ml
scenarios.question: Is this patient taking in enough fluid?
scenarios.text: A fluid chart records what goes in (drinks) and what comes out. The balance is in − out; a negative balance means more out than in. Drinks: 250, 200, 300, 150, 250, 200 ml. Out: 1500 ml (example figures).
steps: Balance: 1350 − 1500 = −150 ml: more out than in, so tell the nurse.

sources.title: NHS (Mersey and West Lancashire), "Fluid input and output (fluid balance): a guide for patients"

scenarios.headline: 19 × 24 = 456 tins
scenarios.question: Has the right delivery arrived?
scenarios.text: Counting stock is where shop staff use maths most. A quick estimate catches a wrong delivery before you sign for it. 19 cases of 24 tins arrive (example figures).
steps: Exact: 19 × 24 = 456. Close to the estimate, so the count looks right.

sources.title: Cambridge Mathematics, "Intersections: Mathematics and the shop floor assistant"

scenarios.headline: 3 × 18 = 54 mph
scenarios.question: Was this car speeding between the cameras?
scenarios.text: Average speed cameras time a car between two cameras a known distance apart. The cameras are 3 miles apart; a car takes 3 min 20 s; the limit is 50 mph (example figures).

steps.text: Time: 3 min 20 s = 200 seconds = 200 ÷ 3600 = 1/18 of an hour.
steps.noCheck: Minutes and seconds ("3 min 20 s") are not read by the check; 200 ÷ 3600 = 1/18 is still recomputed.

sources.title: National Highways, "Average speed enforcement cameras"

scenarios.headline: 13 ÷ 5 = 2.6, so 3 adults
scenarios.question: How many staff does this room legally need?
scenarios.text: By law there must be at least 1 adult for every 5 two-year-olds in a nursery in England. The two-year-olds' room has 13 children.
steps: 13 ÷ 5 = 2.6, and you can't have 0.6 of an adult, so round up: 3 staff.

sources.title: GOV.UK Early Years blog, "How staff-to-child ratios work"

scenarios.headline: 60 − 8 = 52 minutes of programme
scenarios.question: How much of a prime-time hour is your programme?
scenarios.text: On the main commercial channels, adverts between 6 pm and 11 pm may average no more than 8 minutes an hour. An hour slot at 8 minutes of adverts:
steps: Adverts as a share of the hour: 8 ÷ 60 × 100 = 13.3%.

sources.title: Ofcom, "Code on the Scheduling of Television Advertising"

scenarios.headline: √(8² + 2²) = 8.25 m of ladder
scenarios.question: How long a ladder reaches a window 8 m up?
scenarios.text: Ladders go up at 1 out for every 4 up, which HSE says is 75°. A window 8 m up (example figure):
steps: Foot of the ladder out from the wall: 8 ÷ 4 = 2 m.
Angle: tan⁻¹(4) = 75.96°: HSE rounds it to 75°.

sources.title: HSE, "Types of ladder and using them safely"

scenarios.headline: √(3² + 4²) = 5 pixels a frame
scenarios.question: How fast is your character really moving?
scenarios.text: A character moves by a vector each frame. Its speed is the vector's length. The character moves (3, 4) pixels a frame, at 60 frames a second (example figures):

sources.title: National Careers Service, "Computer games developer"
Prospects, "Game developer"

scenarios.headline: 100 × sin 10° = 17.365 mm
scenarios.formulaNote: L is the sine bar's length
scenarios.question: How do you tilt a part to exactly 10°?
scenarios.text: A sine bar sets a part at an exact angle. Its rollers are a fixed distance apart, and a stack of gauge blocks under one roller makes the angle: height = length × sin θ.
steps: A 100 mm sine bar at 10°: 100 × sin 10° = 17.365 mm of blocks.
A 200 mm sine bar at 25°: 200 × sin 25° = 84.52 mm.

sources.title: Hoffmann Group, "Sine bar 100 mm"
Skills England, Machining technician (OCC1305)

scenarios.headline: 50 × cos 120° = −25 mm
scenarios.question: Where exactly do the bolt holes go?
scenarios.text: Bolt holes on a circle (a pitch circle) are programmed as coordinates: x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. Three holes 120° apart on a circle of radius 50 mm (example figures):

sources.title: Omni Calculator, "Bolt circle calculator"

scenarios.headline: 60 ÷ 3 = 20 ml of colour
scenarios.question: How much colour goes in a 60 ml mix?
scenarios.text: Developer strength is sold in "volumes": 10 vol is 3% hydrogen peroxide, so 20 vol is 6%. A common mix is 1 part colour to 2 parts developer. A 60 ml mix at 1 : 2 (example figure):

sources.title: Sally Beauty UK, XP cream developer

scenarios.headline: 8 ÷ 2³ = 1 hour at 94 dB
scenarios.formulaNote: n is the number of 3 dB steps above 85 dB
scenarios.question: How long is safe in a 94 dB workshop?
scenarios.text: Noise is measured in decibels. Every 3 dB more is double the noise, so the safe time halves. At 85 dB the limit is about 8 hours a day.

sources.title: HSE, motor vehicle repair, "Noise"
RNID, "How loud is too loud?"

scenarios.headline: 1000 × 0.10 = 100 m climb
scenarios.question: How far does a 10% hill climb in a kilometre?
scenarios.text: A steep-hill sign shows the gradient as a percentage: 10% is 1 in 10 (1 m up for every 10 m along).
steps: Over 1 km at 10%: 1000 × 0.10 = 100 m of height.

steps.noCheck: "20% is 1 ÷ 0.2" and "1 in 5" put a gradient in words, which the check does not read.

sources.title: GOV.UK, "Know your traffic signs: Warning signs"

scenarios.headline: 2000 ÷ 12 = 166.7 mm
scenarios.question: How high can a 2 m wheelchair ramp rise?
scenarios.text: Building regulations set how steep a wheelchair ramp may be. The shorter the ramp, the steeper it is allowed: 1 : 12 for a 2 m ramp, 1 : 20 for 10 m.
steps: 2 m ramp: 2000 ÷ 12 = 166.7 mm, so the rise can be at most 166 mm (round down: it's a maximum).

sources.title: GOV.UK, Approved Document M, Volume 2 (Table 1, limits for ramp gradients)

scenarios.headline: 64 ÷ 2 = 32 cm drop
scenarios.formulaNote: In cm: down 32 against the strip beside it
scenarios.question: How far down does each strip of half-drop wallpaper move?
scenarios.text: A "half drop" wallpaper's pattern is translated down by half its repeat on every other strip. A 64 cm pattern repeat (the manufacturer's example):
steps: The next strip moves down 64 ÷ 2 = 32 cm.

sources.title: TM Interiors with Arte Wallcoverings, "How to hang half drop repeat wallpaper"

scenarios.headline: 0.02 ÷ 0.01 = 2.0, beyond 1.96
scenarios.question: Has the machine drifted, or is it just chance?
scenarios.text: A shaft should be 25.00 mm. Too big or too small is a fault, so the test is two-tailed. The machine's standard deviation is 0.04 mm; a sample of 16 has a mean of 25.02 mm (example figures). 5% significance, two-tailed: reject if |z| > 1.96.
steps: 2.0 > 1.96, so reject: the machine has drifted. Reset it.

sources.title: Skills England, Quality practitioner (OCC0853, Level 4)

scenarios.question: Is this midfielder's passing any good?
scenarios.text: Analysts turn a match into numbers the coach can use. A midfielder tried 480 passes over five games and 408 reached a teammate (example figures).

sources.title: Skills England, Sport performance analyst (OCC0828)

scenarios.headline: 3² + 4² = 5²
scenarios.question: Is this corner really square?
scenarios.text: To check a corner is square, mark 3 m along one wall and 4 m along the other: the diagonal must be exactly 5 m.
steps: A diagonal of 5.1 m means the corner is more than 90° and the walls aren't square.

sources.title: Wonkee Donkee Tools, "How to lay the first three courses"

scenarios.headline: sin⁻¹(2 ÷ 4) = 30°
scenarios.question: What angle did this blood drop hit at?
scenarios.text: A blood drop that hits a surface at an angle leaves a stretched mark. The width ÷ the length is the sine of the angle it hit at. A mark 2 mm wide and 4 mm long (example figures):
steps: A mark 1 mm by 4 mm: sin⁻¹(0.25) = 14.5°, a shallower hit.

sources.title: Plus Magazine (University of Cambridge), "Solving crimes with maths: Bloodstain pattern analysis"
National Careers Service, "Scenes of crime officer"

scenarios.headline: 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25% of call-backs are cancer
scenarios.question: If you're called back, how likely is it to be cancer?
scenarios.text: NHS breast screening calls about 4 in every 100 people back for more tests. Of those 4, about 1 is diagnosed with breast cancer. Out of 1,000 people screened:
steps: Chance a call-back is cancer: 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%. So 3 in 4 people called back are fine.

sources.title: GOV.UK, "Your guide to NHS breast screening"

scenarios.headline: 1 − 0.0657 = 0.9343, the chance of at least one goal
scenarios.formulaNote: p is each shot's chance of scoring
scenarios.question: Why can't one attack be worth 1.67 goals?
scenarios.text: Expected goals (xG) gives every shot a probability of being scored, from 0 to 1. Different models give slightly different values. One attack had three shots worth 0.41, 0.47 and 0.79 (example figures).
steps: You can't score 1.67 goals from one attack. The chance of no goal is (1 − 0.41) × (1 − 0.47) × (1 − 0.79) = 0.0657, so the chance of at least one goal is 1 − 0.0657 = 0.9343.

sources.title: The Analyst (Opta), "What Is Expected Goals (xG)?"

scenarios.headline: (½)⁴ × 100 = 6.25% left after a day
scenarios.formulaNote: n is the number of half-lives
scenarios.question: How much tracer is left after a day?
scenarios.text: The tracer used in many scans halves every 6 hours (its half-life). After 24 hours:

sources.title: University Hospitals Sussex NHS, "What is nuclear medicine?" (patient information)
British Nuclear Medicine Society, "What does a Nuclear Medicine Technologist do?"

scenarios.headline: 100 × 2⁶ = 6,400 bacteria
scenarios.formulaNote: n is the number of 20-minute doublings
scenarios.question: Why is food left out for 2 hours thrown away?
scenarios.text: Hot food must be kept at 63°C or above. Below that, bacteria can double every 20 minutes in the right conditions, which is why food left out more than 2 hours is thrown away. Start with 100 bacteria, 2 hours at room temperature (example figure):

sources.title: Food Standards Agency, Safer Food Better Business, "Hot holding"
London Borough of Bromley, "High-risk foods"
